cards.front: How do you keep your driving privilege, and what can happen if you do not?
cards.back: A license is a privilege you keep only by continuing to show safe driving skill and knowledge, or it may be restricted, suspended or revoked.

cards.front: What does your driving record list, and who reports it?
cards.back: Your record lists civil or criminal moving violations and crashes, reported to the Secretary of State by police and courts, along with certain drug crimes.

cards.front: What happens to crashes and convictions from other states?
cards.back: Crashes and convictions from other states are reported to Michigan and appear on your record with points assessed under the Michigan system.

cards.front: How long do convictions stay on your record?
cards.back: Most convictions stay on your record for at least seven years, some convictions and licensing actions for at least ten years, and a fatality or impaired driving conviction stays permanently.

cards.front: What does the Driver Privacy Protection Act do with your record details?
cards.back: The Driver Privacy Protection Act keeps personal record details private except for permissible uses set by law, such as insurance rating, vehicle recalls and rental car driver checks.

cards.front: What kinds of traffic violations exist, and what happens if you ignore a ticket?
cards.back: Traffic violations may be civil infractions, misdemeanors or felonies, and ignoring a ticket usually leads to license suspension.

cards.front: What happens if you get a moving violation ticket while suspended?
cards.back: Moving violation tickets received while suspended bring more suspensions and a reinstatement fee.

cards.front: Where must you raise extenuating circumstances for a ticket, and why?
cards.back: Extenuating circumstances for a ticket must be raised in court, because the Secretary of State cannot set aside a court conviction.
cards.memory_hook: tell the court, not the state

cards.front: When are points posted, and how long do they stay?
cards.back: Points, whose values are set in the Michigan Vehicle Code, are posted only after a moving violation conviction and stay on the record for two years from the conviction date.

cards.front: What point totals within two years require a driver assessment reexamination?
cards.back: Six or more one-point violations, or twelve or more points, within a two-year period require a driver assessment reexamination.

cards.front: Are state record points the same as insurance points?
cards.back: State record points are separate from the points an insurance company uses to set your rate.

cards.front: Do state record points set your insurance rate directly?
cards.back: Points on your state driving record are not the same as the points an insurer uses for your rate.

cards.front: How long do points last compared with the convictions behind them?
cards.back: Points drop off after two years, but the convictions behind them stay on the record for at least seven years, some for at least ten, and fatal or impaired driving convictions forever.

cards.front: What two thresholds trigger a reexamination, and over what period?
cards.back: A reexamination is triggered by six or more one-point violations or by twelve or more points, each measured within two years.
cards.memory_hook: six singles, twelve total, two years

cards.front: Name the six-point violations involving felonies, intoxication and leaving a crash.
cards.back: Six-point violations include manslaughter, negligent homicide or another vehicle felony, operating while intoxicated or with any Schedule one drug or cocaine, and failing to stop and identify yourself at a crash.

cards.front: Which other violations, including test refusal and fleeing police, carry six points?
cards.back: Reckless driving, refusing a chemical alcohol test, fleeing or eluding police, and any moving violation causing injury or death also carry six points.

cards.front: What failure to yield carries six points?
cards.back: Failure to yield that causes death or injury to an emergency responder, a construction worker, or a person operating animal husbandry implements carries six points.

cards.front: What are the four-point violations?
cards.back: Four-point violations are drag racing, impaired driving, any bodily alcohol content under age twenty-one, and going sixteen miles per hour or more over the limit.

cards.front: What are the three-point violations?
cards.back: Three-point violations are careless driving, disobeying a signal or stop sign, improper passing, eleven to fifteen miles per hour over the limit, not stopping at a railroad crossing, and not stopping for a school bus or crossing guard.

cards.front: What are the two-point violations?
cards.back: Two-point violations are six to ten miles per hour over the limit, an open alcohol container, a Preliminary Breath Test refusal under twenty-one, failing to yield or use caution for emergency vehicles, and all other moving violations.

cards.front: How do speeding points step up by how far over the limit you go?
cards.back: Speeding points step up by band: six to ten miles per hour over earns two points, eleven to fifteen miles per hour over earns three, and sixteen miles per hour or more over earns four.

cards.front: How do points differ for refusing a chemical test and an underage breath test refusal?
cards.back: Refusing a chemical alcohol test carries six points, while a driver under twenty-one refusing a Preliminary Breath Test gets two points.

cards.front: How do points differ for operating while intoxicated and impaired driving?
cards.back: Operating while intoxicated is a six-point violation, while impaired driving and any bodily alcohol under twenty-one are four-point violations.

cards.front: How do points differ for failing to yield to emergency vehicles and a yield failure that injures a responder?
cards.back: Simply failing to yield to emergency vehicles costs two points, but a failure to yield that kills or injures an emergency responder costs six.

cards.front: Does beer affect you less than wine or whiskey?
cards.back: Beer, wine and whiskey affect you the same way, because a one point five-ounce whiskey shot, a five-ounce wine glass and a twelve-ounce beer can each hold the same amount of alcohol.

cards.front: What does any standard drink affect?
cards.back: Any standard drink affects your judgment and self-control.

cards.front: How can even one drink impair driving?
cards.back: Even one drink can impair driving by slowing reaction time, dulling concentration and causing vision problems.

cards.front: What actually sobers you up?
cards.back: Coffee, cold showers, exercise and fresh air do not sober you up; only time does.

cards.front: What is the best plan for drinking and driving?
cards.back: The best plan is never to drink and drive: choose a sober designated driver in advance, or get a ride, a taxi or public transportation.

cards.front: What should you do when someone is impaired?
cards.back: Never let an impaired person drive or ride with one; take their keys if needed and offer a place to sleep.

cards.front: Do coffee, cold showers, exercise or fresh air remove alcohol's effects?
cards.back: Coffee, a cold shower, exercise or fresh air may feel sobering, but time is the only thing that removes alcohol’s effects.

cards.front: Can a drug conviction suspend your license if you were not driving?
cards.back: Drug convictions require license suspension even if you were not driving, and possession, manufacture or distribution alone can trigger it.

cards.front: How long is the suspension for a first drug violation, and when can a restricted license come?
cards.back: With no prior drug violations the suspension lasts six months, and no restricted license is issued for the first thirty days.

cards.front: How long is the suspension when you have a prior drug conviction within seven years?
cards.back: One or more prior drug convictions within seven years means a one-year suspension with no restricted license for the first sixty days.

cards.front: What is the drug suspension reinstatement fee?
cards.back: The drug suspension reinstatement fee is one hundred twenty-five, dollars separate from any other reinstatement fee.

cards.front: How do first and repeat drug offense suspensions differ?
cards.back: A first drug offense means a six-month suspension with no restricted license for thirty days, while a repeat within seven years means one year with none for sixty days.

cards.front: Is driving impaired by marijuana legal where marijuana is legal?
cards.back: Even where marijuana is legal, driving while impaired by it is illegal and unsafe because it distorts your sense of time, space and speed.

cards.front: How much marijuana may adults twenty-one or older transport?
cards.back: Adults twenty-one or older may legally transport up to two point five ounces of marijuana, with no more than fifteen grams as concentrate.

cards.front: What vehicles may you not operate under the influence of marijuana?
cards.back: It is illegal to operate or be in physical control of a motor vehicle, aircraft, snowmobile, off-road vehicle or motorboat while under the influence of marijuana, or to consume it while doing so.

cards.front: Where is smoking marijuana banned, and can you take it into Canada?
cards.back: Drivers and passengers may not smoke marijuana in a vehicle’s passenger area on a public way, and taking marijuana into Canada is illegal.

cards.front: How do officers judge whether a driver is impaired?
cards.back: Officers judge impairment from your driving, their observations, and standardized and non-standardized field sobriety tests, and may request a chemical test.

cards.front: What is implied consent, and what follows a test refusal?
cards.back: Under the implied consent law, every driver agrees to chemical testing by applying for or renewing a license, and refusing the test brings a license suspension.

cards.front: What penalties come with driving under the influence of marijuana?
cards.back: Driving under the influence of marijuana carries the same penalties as alcohol, including up to ninety-three days in jail, up to a five hundred dollars fine, suspension and six points, with tougher penalties when minors are in the vehicle.

cards.front: How can carrying marijuana be legal while driving under its influence is penalized?
cards.back: Carrying up to two point five ounces of marijuana is legal for adults twenty-one or older, yet driving under its influence carries the same penalties as drunk driving.

cards.front: For what reasons may the Secretary of State reexamine you?
cards.back: The Secretary of State may reexamine you for health concerns, violating license restrictions, crash involvement or a poor driving record.

cards.front: How quickly can probationary and GDL drivers face a reexamination?
cards.back: Probationary and GDL drivers may face a reexamination after just one or two violations.

cards.front: What does a reexamination review and set?
cards.back: A reexamination reviews your driving and sets licensing controls such as restrictions, suspensions, revocations or a mix of them.

cards.front: What are the legal grounds for a reexamination?
cards.back: Legal grounds for reexamination include unfitness or an unsafe physical, visual or mental condition, a fatal crash where the report shows negligence or drinking, and conviction for violating license restrictions.

cards.front: What crash or point counts in two years allow a reexamination?
cards.back: Three or more injury or property-damage crashes in two years, or twelve or more points in two years, also allow a reexamination.

cards.front: What does the driver analyst do at a reexamination?
cards.back: A driver analyst reviews your record with you, and if your license is restricted, suspended or revoked you are told your appeal rights and reinstatement steps.

cards.front: What might a medical reexamination require?
cards.back: A medical reexamination may require vision, written and on-road tests and current medical, vision or psychological information.

cards.front: Where can new drivers and parents find driver education and GDL resources?
cards.back: Michigan.gov slash NewDrivers collects driver education, GDL, parent coaching and teen risk resources.

cards.front: How do reexamination triggers differ for ordinary drivers and new drivers?
cards.back: Ordinary drivers face reexamination at twelve points or three crashes in two years, while probationary and GDL drivers may be called in after one or two violations.

recap_hooks.text: Your record lists violations, crashes and some drug crimes, including those from other states.
Most convictions stay seven years, some ten, and fatal or impaired ones forever.
Points post at conviction and last two years; twelve points or six one-point violations bring a reexam.
State points are not insurance points.
Six for the gravest offenses, four for impaired and big speeding, three for signals and buses, two for the rest.
Speeding steps up two, three, four by band.
A drink is a drink, one drink slows you, and only time sobers.
Plan a sober ride and take the keys from anyone impaired.
Drug convictions suspend licenses even without driving: six months first, one year for a repeat.
Carrying marijuana can be legal; driving high carries the same penalties as alcohol.
Applying for a license means consenting to chemical tests.
Twelve points or three crashes in two years can mean a reexam; new drivers can be called after one or two violations.
